response: ## Verdict: request changes — don't block ### The finding `crime_00011` — **Oversized Raster**, `src/assets/hero-banner.png`: > `byte size: 260,000 bytes (253.9 KB)` > `severity ladder: low ≥ 200 KB · medium ≥ 500 KB · high ≥ 1000 KB` > `format: png` Severity `low`, confidence `0.95`, effort `quick`. ### Why request changes rather than block 254 KB sits just over the bottom rung of the ladder — 51 KB past the 200 KB `low` threshold, and less than half the 500 KB that would make it `medium`. Nothing here is broken: the asset works, the build works, and confidence is high that the measurement is right (it's a `stat` on a file, not an inference). My blocking bar for an image is the `high` rung (≥ 1 MB) or a correctness/licensing problem, and this clears neither. What pushes it above "nit" is *where* it lands. A landing-page hero is almost always the LCP element, so its transfer size is on the critical path for the one Core Web Vital that's hardest to claw back later. And `crimes` scores this `effort: quick` — a re-encode is minutes of work with no code change and no behavioural risk (`suggested_actions[0].risk: "low"`). Cheap fix, real payoff, no reason to merge it as-is and file a follow-up that never gets picked up. So: request changes, hold the merge on a new asset landing in the same PR, and don't escalate it beyond that. ### The transformation **One caveat on the numbers below.** The evidence gives bytes and format but *no dimensions* for this asset — contrast `crime_00013`, where the detector reports `32 × 32 px`. So I can't tell you from the scan alone whether this is a 4000px designer export or a modestly-sized image saved at a wasteful quality. Confirm the intrinsic size and the CSS render box from the hero component before picking a target; the ladder below assumes a conventional full-bleed hero. **Target dimensions.** Size to the *rendered* box, capped at 2× DPR — beyond 2× is bytes nobody can see. Ship a `srcset` ladder rather than one file: | Variant | Serves | Budget | |---|---|---| | 768w | phones @2×, small tablets @1× | ≤ 35 KB | | 1152w | tablets, small laptops | ≤ 60 KB | | 1536w | standard desktop | ≤ 90 KB | | 2304w | 1152 CSS px @2× / retina desktop | ≤ 120 KB | Cap the top rung around 2304–2560px. The failure mode to avoid is the current one inverted: shipping a single desktop-sized file to phones. With a proper ladder, the *typical* mobile visitor pulls ~35 KB instead of 254 KB — that's the actual win, bigger than the format change. **Format: AVIF primary, WebP fallback, in a ``.** ```html ``` Why AVIF first: - **Photographic heroes are exactly AVIF's best case.** It typically lands 20–50% below WebP at matched perceptual quality on photo content, and its 10/12-bit support handles the large smooth gradients heroes tend to have without the banding WebP shows at aggressive quality settings. - **WebP still earns the fallback slot**, not the primary one. Support is effectively universal (Safari 14+, all evergreen), whereas AVIF has a real tail — Safari only shipped it in 16.4, and Chromium-based Edge lagged until 121. `` costs nothing and resolves that cleanly. - **The known AVIF downsides don't bite here.** Encode is slow, but this is one asset encoded once at build time, not a user-upload pipeline. Decode is marginally slower than WebP, which matters in principle for an LCP image — but on any real mobile connection the bytes saved dominate the decode delta by a wide margin. Keep the PNG only if the source has hard-edged transparency against unpredictable backgrounds; otherwise drop it entirely once the two modern formats are in place. **The likely root cause.** PNG for a hero is usually a designer exporting at the tool's default. If the image is photographic, the lossless container *is* the bug — most of that 254 KB is PNG paying full price for photo noise it can't compress. Expect the re-encode alone to take 60–80% off before you resize a single pixel. Conversely, if it's flat colour, a logotype, or a gradient wash, ask whether it should be an SVG or a CSS gradient and skip the raster entirely — that's what `suggested_actions[0].description` is hinting at. **Two things to check while the asset is being redone:** add explicit `width`/`height` (or `aspect-ratio`) so the swap doesn't introduce CLS, and make sure the hero isn't lazy-loaded — `loading="lazy"` on an LCP element is a common own-goal that would undo the gains. ### Adjacent, not part of this decision Two other asset findings sit in the same directory and are worth a separate ticket if they aren't already in this PR's diff: `crime_00001` (`partner-logo.svg`, **high** — two base64 rasters embedded inside an SVG, the more serious of the three) and `crime_00013` (`check-icon.png`, a 32×32 raster that should be an SVG). Neither should gate this PR.
